1.pericope_label: The counsel to gather fair young virgins, and the office set over the house of the women

schools.summary: Gill offers two accounts of the interval since the feast: that the king’s wrath went off with his wine, so that it was a few days at most, or else that the gap covers the expedition of Xerxes into Greece, from which he returned to Shushan in the seventh year of his reign and married Esther that year; he adds that after the expedition the king gave himself up to his amours and on the road to Sardis fell in love with his brother’s wife. Of the courtiers he supposes they feared vengeance would be taken on them if Vashti were restored, or at least wished to remove the king’s grief and melancholy; and of the officers to be appointed he notes that they best knew where beautiful virgins might be found in their own provinces.

Ellicott fixes the limits by dates, the great feast at Susa falling in one year and the setting out for Greece two years later, so that the proposal belongs somewhere between them; the marriage itself did not come about until after the return from Greece, the king’s long absence explaining a delay that would otherwise be curious, and even in that interval he was entangled in more than one illicit connection. He identifies the house of the women as the harem, then as now a prominent feature in the establishment of an Eastern king, and distinguishes the two eunuchs, the one here named having charge of the virgins while another named later had the custody of the concubines. The whole verse, he adds, shows as conclusively as anything could in how degrading an aspect Eastern women were viewed. Keil and Delitzsch summarise the sequence, that when the king’s wrath was appeased and he remembered his harsh treatment of Vashti his courtiers proposed fetching fair young virgins from all parts of the realm to the house of the women in Susa, that he might choose a new queen from among them, and that the proposal pleased him and was acted upon.

Clarke describes without euphemism what was being set up: this was the usual way in which the harem was furnished, the finest women in the land, whether of high or low birth, being sought out and brought in, so that they all became the king’s concubines, one only being raised as chief wife to the throne, whose issue was specially entitled to inherit. He notes that the officer is called the king’s eunuch by the Septuagint and Vulgate and Targum and Syriac alike, since in Eastern countries the women are entrusted to eunuchs only, and identifies the things for purification as cosmetics, the oil of myrrh and sweet odours named later in the chapter. Wesley makes the same officer keeper of all the women, both virgins and concubines, who took the virgins into his own care as requiring more caution and committed the concubines to the other man as his deputy; and of the purification he observes that it was to cleanse and perfume and adorn and every way prepare them for the king, while for the legal purification of the Jews he never regarded it.

Henry sets the chapter under a frame drawn from two songs: we have read in the chapter before how God put down one that was high and mighty from her seat, and are now to be told how he exalted one of low degree, as the virgin Mary observes in her song and Hannah before her — Vashti being humbled for her height, Esther is advanced for her humility. He reports from Josephus that when the king’s anger was over he was exceedingly grieved the matter had been carried so far, and calls the remedy an extravagant course taken to please him with another wife instead.

5.pericope_label: Mordecai the Jew and Hadassah his cousin, taken into the house of the women and finding favour

schools.summary: Ellicott says the antecedent of the clause about the captivity is obviously Kish, though as far as the mere grammar goes it might have been Mordecai, and supports it by arithmetic, the deportation under Nebuchadnezzar falling more than a century before this time so that the four generations of the pedigree are readily accounted for. He passes on Canon Rawlinson’s identification of Mordecai with Matacas, the most powerful of the eunuchs in the reign of Xerxes, and argues that Mordecai may be assumed to have been a eunuch himself from the way he is allowed access to the royal harem; the name, he notes, occurs among those who returned with Zerubbabel. On the two names he takes Hadassah from the Hebrew for myrtle and says Esther is generally assumed to be Persian for a star, drawing the wider inference that unless the second name was given afterwards and used here by anticipation we have an early instance of the common Jewish practice of bearing a Hebrew and a Gentile name together, as Saul and Paul or John and Mark. Keil and Delitzsch gloss Mordecai’s relation as foster-father, give Hadassah as a myrtle and compare the Greek women’s names formed from the same plant, and derive Esther from an Old Persian word for star with a prosthetic letter, answering to the Greek and to the modern Persian.

Gill reaches the same conclusion as Ellicott about the captivity from the absurdity of the alternative: otherwise Mordecai must be a very old man and Esther, his first cousin and the child of his father’s brother, must be at an age one would not reckon among young virgins nor think so amiable, and according to the former Targum she was seventy-five years old. He explains that Mordecai is called a Jew not as of the tribe of Judah, since he is afterwards called a Benjaminite, but as of the kingdom of Judah which consisted of both tribes, citing Jarchi that all carried captive with the kings of Judah were called Jews among the nations. Of the names he takes Hadassah for a myrtle, to which Israelites and good men are sometimes compared, and offers for the other a Hebrew root meaning to hide, because she was hidden in Mordecai’s house, before allowing the Persian sense. On the concealment of her kindred he makes it lawful rather than merely prudent, since the question was not asked and she was under no obligation to declare it, being taken for a Persian as one born in Shushan; and he is careful that the maiden pleased the chamberlain, not yet the king, into whose presence she had not been introduced.

Clarke gives the Targum’s pedigree and the legend attached to it, that the Shimei in the line was the same who cursed David, whom David forbade Joab to kill because he saw in the spirit of prophecy that he was to be the ancestor of Esther and Mordecai, but whom, when he grew old and past having children, David ordered Solomon to put to death. He takes Hadassah for a myrtle in Chaldee, probably her first or Babylonish name, and Esther for a star in Persian, calling the name undoubtedly Persian; and he settles the kinship, that she was daughter of Mordecai’s uncle and therefore his cousin, though the Vulgate and Josephus make her his niece, it being safest to follow the Hebrew. Her favour with the keeper he credits to the propriety of her deportment and her engaging though unassuming manners, and he explains the seven maidens as attendants for the bath and the anointing. The concealment he makes prudent and necessary: it was no credit at the Persian court to be a Jew, and had her lineage been known envy might have prevented her ever having access to the king. Wesley settles the order of the names simply, that Hadassah was hers before the marriage and Esther what the king called her after, and adds to the favour she found a cause the others leave out, the divine power which moves the hearts of men whichever way it pleases.

12.pericope_label: The twelve months of purification, Esther taken in to the king, and crowned queen instead of Vashti

schools.summary: Clarke offers a reason for the twelve months which he claims no writer he has seen has apprehended: the most beautiful virgins of all the provinces were selected indiscriminately out of every class of the people, so that many must have been brought up in low life on coarse and strong food, and it is on that ground that so long a course of oil and ointments was needed before they were fit to be presented. He explains the provision of whatever each desired, that any kind of dress or stuff or colour or jewels she thought best to set off her person should be given her; says the second house was where the concubines were kept, who went out no more and were never given in marriage to any man and saw the king’s face no more unless specially called; and offers two Persian etymologies for the keeper’s name, one meaning beardless and the other weak loins, either being a fit epithet for a eunuch, remarking that names of this kind show at once the reason of their imposition. He gives the month as answering to part of our December and January, and describes the crowning in the terms of his own day, that she was made what is now called in the East the Sultana, mistress of all the rest of the wives, who were obliged to pay her the most profound respect. Wesley takes the permission of ornament or attendance and then adds a defence of her position the others do not attempt: every one whom the king took to his bed was his wife of a lower rank, as Hagar was Abraham’s, so that it would have been no sin nor dishonour to Esther even had she not been made queen.

Keil and Delitzsch give the division of the time without comment, six months with oil of myrrh and six with balsam and ointments of purification, and mark the contrast when Esther’s turn came, that she required nothing to take with her but what the keeper of the women appointed. Ellicott corrects the single word, that what the version calls the manner of women should be rendered law or ordinance, and notes that the phrase for obtaining kindness here is the same that is rendered obtaining favour later in the chapter. He places the marriage in the January or February of a particular year, observing that the month named occurs only here and comparing the Egyptian month of similar name, and draws a conclusion from it: this must have been very shortly after Xerxes returned to Susa from the West, which accounts for the long delay in replacing Vashti.

Gill explains the order of presentation, that the virgins came in by turns according to the length of time they had been in the house, as he says Herodotus relates of the wives of the Persian kings. Of the second house he agrees it was the other apartment where those the king had made his secondary wives were kept, but reports that Aben Ezra takes the word not of a second house at all but of a second time, and that the Targum renders it again. He marks the difference between Esther and the rest, that she did not return on the morrow as those who became only concubines did, but was taken to be his wife and designed for his queen; he gives her father’s name as Abihail and not as the Septuagint has it; and he notes that Jarchi understood the women she was preferred above to be married women, supposing such were gathered as well as virgins.

19.pericope_label: Mordecai in the king’s gate discovers the plot of Bigthan and Teresh, and it is written in the chronicles

schools.summary: Gill rejects the suggestion that the second gathering looks back to a collection made when Vashti was chosen, since there is no proof any such collection was then made, and concludes instead that the king’s lust was such that he gathered them again although he already had a queen. On Esther’s continued silence he notes that she had not disclosed her kindred since being made queen any more than before, though according to the Targums the king himself urged her to it; and he takes Mordecai’s sitting in the gate as the posture of an officer at court.

Ellicott reaches Gill’s judgment about the king from the chronology instead: the incident cannot be dated precisely, falling somewhere between the marriage and the twelfth year of the reign, but since Esther had been his wife certainly less and possibly much less than five years, the fact of a second gathering shows how the word love is degraded in this connection. On her silence he suggests the verse may be added to meet the supposition that the king would have wished to replace her had he discovered her nation. The discovery of the plot he reads for its consequence, that by this means an increased influence was doubtless gained over the capricious mind of the king, an influence which before long served Esther in good stead. The execution he takes for crucifixion, a punishment common among the Persians and especially used on rebels, citing the crucifying of the dead body of Leonidas by Xerxes’ orders after the desperate stand at Thermopylae; and of the record he notes that a sleepless night would afterwards bring the book of the chronicles to be read. Keil and Delitzsch mark only the function of the passage, that it relates an incident of great importance for the later development of the narrative, two courtiers being incensed with the king and seeking to lay hands on him, which came to the knowledge of Mordecai as he sat in the gate of the palace.

Clarke settles what Mordecai was doing in the gate by an argument from what happens later: he may have been one of the king’s officers, the gate being where such men attended to await the royal call, and it is not likely he was the porter, for had he been only that, Haman could have removed him at once. Of the conspirators he says plainly that we are not informed of their motive, reports the Targum’s account that they had discovered something concerning Esther, and notes that they were eunuchs. On how the plot came to light he passes on Josephus, that a Jew overheard it and told Mordecai, who told Esther, who told the king in Mordecai’s name, so that Mordecai was registered as the discoverer. The execution he suspects was not hanging but impaling, and describes the manner at length, a pointed stake set upright in the ground and the culprit placed upon its point and drawn down by the legs. Wesley agrees that Mordecai sat there by office, as one of the king’s guards or ministers, and adds that he had been advanced to the place by Esther’s favour.

Henry reads the whole incident as narrative architecture. The good service is recorded here because the mention of it will occur again to Mordecai’s advantage; and though no step is yet taken towards the design of the Jews’ destruction, several steps are already taken towards God’s design of their deliverance, this being one — God giving Mordecai an opportunity of doing the king a good turn beforehand, that he might have it to plead when it was wanted.
